title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 21
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: An airline introduced tiered loyalty status and reports that members who reach its highest tier fly more than other members. It concludes that the status scheme increases flying.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Higher tiers offer lounge access.
B. Status is awarded on the basis of miles flown during the year.
C. Some members hold status with several airlines.
D. The airline operates a large network.
E. Status can be retained for one year after qualification.
questions.explanation: The tier is defined by the behaviour it is claimed to cause, so the association is guaranteed by the scheme's own rules and carries no causal information.

questions.prompt: A government offering grants for home insulation reports that households receiving grants reduced their gas consumption by 20 per cent. It concludes that insulation reduces consumption by that amount.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Grants covered only part of the cost of the work.
B. The insulation is expected to last decades.
C. Some households installed insulation without a grant.
D. Gas prices rose during the period.
E. Households applied for grants when their heating bills had become unusually high, and consumption in comparable non-applying households also fell, though by less.
questions.explanation: Applying at a peak means part of the fall is regression toward a normal level, and the non-applying comparison shows some of the drop occurred without insulation.

questions.prompt: A hospital trust recruited nurses from overseas and reports that its vacancy rate fell. A critic argues that the policy may not be sustainable.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most supports the critic's argument?
options: A. Overseas nurses require an induction programme.
B. Recruitment agencies charge a fee per placement.
C. The trust also raised its pay for senior nurses.
D. Two-thirds of the recruited nurses left within three years, most moving to other employers in the same country once their initial contracts ended.
E. Vacancy rates vary between wards.
questions.explanation: High onward turnover means the vacancy improvement is temporary and the recruitment must be repeated, which is exactly a sustainability objection.

questions.prompt: A seed library lends vegetable seeds and asks borrowers to return seed from the plants they grow. It reports that returned seed has a germination rate lower than the seed originally lent, and concludes that home growers save seed badly.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How many borrowers use the library
B. Whether borrowers pay a membership fee
C. Whether the returned seed is stored under the same conditions as the original stock before testing
D. How the library advertises its service
E. Whether vegetables grown from returned seed taste different
questions.explanation: If the two batches are tested after different storage, the comparison measures handling by the library as much as saving by the growers.

questions.prompt: Every restaurant in the Ashdene district that lists on a delivery application also offers a takeaway collection service. No restaurant offering collection has closed in the past two years. Some restaurants in the district have closed in the past two years.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some restaurants in the district do not list on a delivery application.
B. Delivery applications keep restaurants open.
C. Most restaurants offer collection.
D. No restaurant listing on an application will close.
E. Restaurants that closed had poor reviews.
questions.explanation: Closed restaurants offered no collection, and listing on an application implies collection, so the closed ones did not list. B and D overstate what follows.

questions.prompt: A taxi company replaced its fleet with electric vehicles and reports that its fuel and energy costs per mile fell by 60 per cent. It concludes that the change has reduced its total operating costs proportionately.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the environmental benefits of the change
B. treats a fall in one component of cost as a proportionate fall in total cost
C. assumes electricity prices will remain stable
D. does not specify the size of the fleet
E. overlooks driver preferences
questions.explanation: Energy is one input among vehicle finance, insurance, maintenance and driver pay, so a 60 per cent fall in it cannot be carried across to the total.

questions.prompt: A council offering grants for school uniforms reports that applications rose 40 per cent after it simplified the form, and concludes that the complexity of the form had been excluding eligible families.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The new form is available online.
B. The grant amount was unchanged.
C. Families who had abandoned partly completed applications under the old form account for most of the increase, and the council's estimate of eligible families is unchanged.
D. Council staff were trained on the new process.
E. Neighbouring councils have similar schemes.
questions.explanation: It identifies the increase as coming from people the old process had turned away, and holds eligibility constant so the rise is not simply more eligible families.

questions.prompt: An animal charity reports that dogs rehomed to households with previous dog experience are returned less often than those rehomed to first-time owners, and proposes to rehome only to experienced households.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal?
options: A. First-time owners often seek advice from the charity.
B. Experienced owners tend to be older.
C. Some returns are caused by changes in the owner's circumstances.
D. The charity rehomes several hundred dogs a year.
E. The charity already places its most difficult dogs with first-time owners, because experienced households are unwilling to take them.
questions.explanation: The placement rule attributes to owner experience a difference produced by which dogs each group receives: if the hardest dogs go to first-time owners, the return-rate gap reflects the dogs, and restricting rehoming would leave those dogs unplaced.

questions.prompt: A warehouse introduced a system that directs pickers to items by the shortest route and reports that items picked per hour rose by 12 per cent. It concludes that the system has made picking more efficient.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Pickers wear headsets to receive instructions.
B. The system cost less than a warehouse redesign.
C. Some pickers ignore the suggested route.
D. Picking errors rose sharply, and the time spent by other staff correcting them exceeds the time the pickers saved.
E. Item locations are updated weekly.
questions.explanation: Efficiency is a claim about the whole operation; work moved to another team at a higher cost is not a saving.

questions.prompt: An insurer raised the excess on its home policies and reports that the number of claims fell by a quarter. It concludes that a quarter of previous claims had been unnecessary.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that claims not made were claims not worth making
B. ignores the effect on customer satisfaction
C. does not report the size of the excess
D. relies on a single year of data
E. overlooks claims made under other policies
questions.explanation: A higher excess suppresses small genuine claims along with any unnecessary ones; the fall says nothing about which kind was deterred.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to fund free school meals for all pupils argue that it will improve attainment, citing studies of means-tested schemes. Opponents reply that most pupils already receive adequate meals, so the additional spending will buy little.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' reply?
options: A. Universal schemes are simpler to administer.
B. In areas that moved from means-tested to universal provision, attainment rose most among pupils who had been eligible but not claiming, whose numbers were far larger than expected.
C. Some parents object to the meals offered.
D. Free meals reduce family expenditure.
E. The cost per meal falls as more meals are served.
questions.explanation: It identifies a large group whose meals were not in fact adequate and whom means testing failed to reach, which is precisely the premise the reply rests on.

questions.passageText:
An audit exists to give people outside a company confidence in the accounts. It is commissioned and paid for by the company being audited. The arrangement is so familiar that its oddity passes unnoticed, and most of the profession's regulation is an attempt to manage a conflict that the payment structure creates rather than to remove it.

The pressure is not usually crude. An auditor who takes a hard line on a judgement risks losing a client whose fee is material to the firm, and the incentive operates on the marginal decision — how much evidence to require for a valuation, whether to escalate a disagreement — rather than on outright falsification. Because those judgements are numerous and individually defensible, the effect is difficult to observe in any single case and shows up in aggregate patterns.

The remedies attempted are instructive in their partiality. Mandatory rotation of audit firms limits the value of any one relationship but discards accumulated knowledge of a complex business. Separating audit from consultancy removes one channel of dependence, and the evidence that it changes audit quality is mixed. Restricting an auditor's staff from joining the client addresses a real route of influence and is easily circumvented by timing.

The arrangement that would resolve the conflict — payment by the users of the accounts, or by a levy administered independently of the company — is proposed periodically and has not been adopted at scale, for reasons that include genuine difficulty in specifying who the users are. Until then, an audit opinion should be read as the product of a system that has been designed to contain a conflict rather than one that lacks it.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the conflict in the audit relationship operates chiefly through
options: A. outright falsification of accounts
B. the auditor's ownership of shares in the client
C. regulators' reluctance to impose penalties
D. marginal judgements such as how much evidence to require or whether to escalate a disagreement
E. disagreements between audit partners
questions.explanation: The passage stresses the pressure is not usually crude and that the effect appears in aggregate patterns rather than single cases.

questions.passageText:
Several techniques long presented in court as identification evidence have been found, on examination, to rest on much less than their courtroom presentation implied. The pattern of those failures is more informative than any single technique's fate.

Comparison methods — of bite marks, hair, tool marks, and to a lesser extent fingerprints — developed within investigative institutions rather than research ones. Practitioners were trained by other practitioners, proficiency was judged by experienced colleagues, and the central claim, that a feature could be matched to one source to the exclusion of all others, was rarely subjected to a test in which the examiner did not know what answer was expected. Reviews in the last two decades found that some techniques had no established error rate at all, and that examiners' conclusions could be influenced by contextual information about the case.

The response has been uneven. Some techniques have been abandoned, others reformed with blind verification, standardised terminology, and reporting that states a probability rather than an identification. Fingerprint and firearms examination remain in use with substantially altered claims.

The wider lesson concerns what a court can assess. A jury asked to weigh an expert's confidence has no way to test whether that confidence is calibrated, and adversarial cross-examination is a poor instrument for the purpose, since it probes the witness rather than the method. Institutions that certify a technique before it reaches court do the work that the trial itself cannot do — which is why the failures were discovered by scientific review rather than by the process that had been relying on them for decades.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, comparison techniques developed within
options: A. investigative institutions rather than research ones
B. university research departments
C. commercial testing laboratories
D. the courts themselves
E. international standards bodies
questions.explanation: The passage links this origin to training by practitioners and proficiency judged by colleagues.

questions.passageText:
Wealth is distributed far more unequally than income in every country that measures both, and inheritance is central to how that distribution persists. Its effects are frequently misdescribed in both directions.

The first misdescription treats inheritance as the main source of wealth inequality among the living. Most large fortunes in most periods were accumulated within a lifetime, and inherited wealth is a smaller share of total wealth than its prominence in public argument suggests. The second, and more common in economics, treats inheritance as a modest transfer that dissipates across generations as estates divide among heirs. That understates it, because inheritance operates less through the transfer of large sums than through what modest transfers permit: a deposit on a house, an unpaid internship, a business that does not have to succeed immediately.

Those advantages compound and are largely invisible in the estate statistics. Two people with identical incomes and different parents face different risks, and the one who can fail without consequence takes the opportunities that require the possibility of failure.

The measurement problem is severe. Transfers during life are poorly recorded, housing wealth is unevenly valued, and the households at the top are precisely those least well captured by surveys. Estimates of inheritance's contribution to inequality therefore vary widely with method, and the honest position is that its role is substantial, understated by the visible transfers, and not the whole of what produces the distribution — three claims that are regularly collapsed into whichever one supports the argument being made.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the first misdescription of inheritance is the claim that it is
options: A. a modest transfer that dissipates across generations
B. impossible to measure
C. the main source of wealth inequality among the living
D. concentrated in housing wealth
E. declining in importance
questions.explanation: Most large fortunes in most periods were accumulated within a lifetime, which is the passage's answer to that claim.

questions.passageText:
The white marble of classical sculpture is an accident of survival. Greek and Roman statues were painted, often in strong colours, and traces of that paint survive in quantities sufficient to reconstruct the schemes with reasonable confidence.

The evidence is of several kinds. Pigment residues persist in protected areas — undercuts, folds, the interiors of nostrils. Raking light reveals weathering patterns in which painted areas eroded differently from bare stone. Ultraviolet fluorescence and spectroscopic analysis identify compounds without removing material. And ancient texts refer to the painting of statues as unremarkable, which is what a practice looks like when everyone knows about it.

The resistance to this evidence is the interesting part. Reconstructions, when exhibited, are routinely described as garish, and the objection is usually aesthetic rather than evidential — the colours are said to look wrong. That reaction has a history: the taste for white marble was formed in a period when the surviving objects had been white for a thousand years, and the neoclassical aesthetic built on that appearance was then read back onto the ancient world as its intention.

Two cautions belong in the reconstruction. Surviving traces are partial, so the intensity and blending of tones involve judgement, and early reconstructions using flat colour probably overstated the crudeness of the originals. But the choice is not between a reconstruction and the truth; it is between a reconstruction that states its evidence and a white statue, which is also a reconstruction, and one whose confident familiarity conceals that it is wrong.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, evidence for the painting of classical sculpture includes all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. pigment residues in protected areas such as folds and undercuts
B. unpainted copies made for export
C. weathering differences visible under raking light
D. spectroscopic identification of compounds
E. ancient texts treating the practice as unremarkable
questions.explanation: The first four are the categories the passage lists; export copies are not mentioned.

Those advantages compound and are largely invisible in the estate statistics. Two people with identical incomes and different parents face different risks, and the one who can fail without consequence takes the opportunities that require the possibility of failure.

The measurement problem is severe. Transfers during life are poorly recorded, housing wealth is unevenly valued, and the households at the top are precisely those least well captured by surveys. Estimates of inheritance's contribution to inequality therefore vary widely with method, and the honest position is that its role is substantial, understated by the visible transfers, and not the whole of what produces the distribution — three claims that are regularly collapsed into whichever one supports the argument being made.

readingPassages.title: The Colours of Antiquity
readingPassages.text:
The white marble of classical sculpture is an accident of survival. Greek and Roman statues were painted, often in strong colours, and traces of that paint survive in quantities sufficient to reconstruct the schemes with reasonable confidence.

The evidence is of several kinds. Pigment residues persist in protected areas — undercuts, folds, the interiors of nostrils. Raking light reveals weathering patterns in which painted areas eroded differently from bare stone. Ultraviolet fluorescence and spectroscopic analysis identify compounds without removing material. And ancient texts refer to the painting of statues as unremarkable, which is what a practice looks like when everyone knows about it.

The resistance to this evidence is the interesting part. Reconstructions, when exhibited, are routinely described as garish, and the objection is usually aesthetic rather than evidential — the colours are said to look wrong. That reaction has a history: the taste for white marble was formed in a period when the surviving objects had been white for a thousand years, and the neoclassical aesthetic built on that appearance was then read back onto the ancient world as its intention.

Two cautions belong in the reconstruction. Surviving traces are partial, so the intensity and blending of tones involve judgement, and early reconstructions using flat colour probably overstated the crudeness of the originals. But the choice is not between a reconstruction and the truth; it is between a reconstruction that states its evidence and a white statue, which is also a reconstruction, and one whose confident familiarity conceals that it is wrong.
